title: Fragmented Britain: Seventh Prime Minister in a Decade
author: Deepak Tripathi
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/10_Downing_Street._MOD_45155532-680x394.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/27/fragmented-
britain-seventh-prime-minister-in-a-decade/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/10_Downing_Street._MOD_45155532-680x394.jpg)

Photograph Source: Sergeant Tom Robinson RLC/MOD - [OGL
v1.0](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-
licence/version/1/open-government-licence.htm)

Just two years after the July 4, 2024, general election, in which Kier Starmer
led the Labour Party to a landslide victory, his party has forced him out as
prime minister. Andy Burnham has succeeded him, becoming the [seventh prime
minister](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/news-wrap-andy-burnham-becomes-
britains-7th-prime-minister-in-a-decade) of the United Kingdom in a decade –
an unprecedented frequency of change of government in modern Britain. Under
Starmer, Labour ended [14 years of Conservative Party
rule](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/boris-johnson-david-cameron-
theresa-may-liz-truss-george-osborne-b2573683.html), during which the
Conservatives had five different prime ministers and had become associated
with instability in domestic politics and foreign relations. The events
surrounding Starmer’s short tenure in the Prime Minister’s official residence
Downing Street and controversies that forced his resignation indicate that
Labour may now be on a similar path.

This is particularly striking given that the party won an overwhelming
parliamentary majority in 2024, securing [412 of the 650
seats](https://www.bbc.com/news/election/2024/uk/results) in the House of
Commons. A governing party elected with one of the strongest mandates in
modern history now appears to be grappling with the same volatility that
weakened the Conservatives. Burnham has already created a distinct “Starmer
faction” within the Labour parliamentary Party by dismissing a large number of
Starmer’s cabinet members, including Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy and
Chancellor of the Exchequer (Finance Minister) Rachael Reeves, in one of the
[most sweeping cabinet
reshuffles](https://www.thenational.scot/news/26295648.full-list-keir-
starmers-sacked-cabinet-andy-burnham/) in recent British political history.

The political system in the United Kingdom has not been the same since the
Brexit referendum in June 2016, when the British electorate voted by a [narrow
margin](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/politics/eu_referendum/results) to leave
the European Union. Prime Minister David Cameron had called the referendum in
the expectation that voters would reject Brexit, thereby settling the issue
once and for all. Instead, the result exposed deep divisions within both the
Conservative Party and British society. Cameron became the first political
casualty, [resigning as prime minister](https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-
eu-referendum-36619446) and later as an MP. The referendum had a lasting
destabilizing effect on British politics from which the country has yet to
recover. Cameron was succeeded by Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, and
Rishi Sunak, none of whom remained in office long enough to complete a normal
five-year parliamentary term. Each prime minister struggled with political
crises, internal party divisions, or economic challenges that ultimately ended
their premiership.

Labour’s decisive victory in the 2024 general election was expected to restore
political stability, but events since then suggest otherwise. The forces
unleashed by Brexit, combined with the rise of populism and growing anti-
government and anti-establishment sentiment across many democracies, continue
to affect British politics. Britain remains one of the countries most deeply
affected by these trends.

The two main British political parties – the Labour Party and the Conservative
Party – which have traditionally alternated in government, are deeply divided
over a wide range of domestic and foreign policy issues. The Reform Party, led
by the right-wing populist Nigel Farage, has evolved through several
incarnations since its origins in the campaign for Brexit and now competes
with both Labour and Conservatives in opinion polls. The 2016 Brexit
referendum fundamentally changed British politics. Voters, having tasted power
themselves, are determined to exercise the way they feel they did in the
Brexit referendum. And politicians seeking elected office feel compelled to
respond to the preferences of the groups most likely to ensure the outcome in
their favor. British politics has undergone a fundamental shift, with
established patterns of decision-making giving way to more fragmented and
volatile politics.

Kier Starmer came to power with great fanfare. After 14 years in office and
five prime ministers, the Conservatives had exhausted themselves, and much of
the country was ready for change. A former Director of Public Prosecutions for
England and Wales, Starmer brought legal gravitas and an outsider’s reputation
to Downing Street, despite his proximity to the corridors of power. Yet he
soon appeared unable to hold together the broad coalition of views and
priorities that a successful leader of a major political party must manage. A
London-based lawyer representing a London constituency, he never developed a
coherent governing vision that reached beyond Westminster. In the absence of
such a platform, Labour’s popularity collapsed, members drifted to the Greens
and Liberal Democrats, and many who remained became increasingly
disillusioned.

Prime Minister Starmer’s government compounded its political problems with a
series of avoidable mistakes. The most damaging was the appointment of Peter
Mandelson as Britain’s ambassador to Washington despite [longstanding
questions](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz9vz8d0n85o) about his
association with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. When further
evidence of those links emerged, Starmer was forced into the humiliating
position of [dismissing](https://news.sky.com/story/keir-starmer-sacks-
mandelson-as-us-ambassador-over-epstein-ties-13427982) his own ambassador,
reinforcing the impression of a government short in judgment as well as
direction. Open rebellion erupted within the parliamentary Labour Party and
spread throughout the wider party. As growing numbers of Labour MPs, including
members of his own cabinet, concluded that his leadership had become
untenable, pressure mounted on him to step aside. Once it became clear that he
no longer commanded the confidence of either his parliamentary colleagues or
much of his party membership, Starmer had little choice but to accept the
inevitable. He announced his
[resignation](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/what-happens-if-uks-starmer-
quits-or-is-challenged-2026-06-22/), bringing to an abrupt end a premiership
that had begun with high expectations but quickly dissolved into
disappointment.

The question now is whether Andy Burnham, Britain’s seventh prime minister in
a decade, will do better. Burnham faces a formidable task in his new job. As
Mayor of Greater Manchester, a directly elected position in one of the largest
strategic authorities outside London, Burnham was a popular figure. However,
being Prime Minister of the United Kingdom is a colossal responsibility. In a
highly complex international environment, he remains untested in foreign
affairs and diplomacy, and whether he succeeds remains to be seen. On the
domestic front, he has established himself as a “[people
pleaser](https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/andy-burnham-tax-cuts-people-
pleaser-labour-b3013128.html).” He has already
[backtracked](https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/andy-burnham-prime-
minister-government-chris-bryant-wes-streeting-b1290910.html) on his initial
suggestion to increase the income tax-free personal allowance. His immediate
announcement to cut VAT on household electricity bills has been dismissed as
unfunded by [Darren Jones](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c62xzn3j1p2o), a
minister in Starmer’s cabinet who was fired by Burnham. And he says he wishes
to deliver [power to every
postcode](https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/26294614.burnham-pledges-carry-
power-every-postcode/). So far, his promise to reduce the [bus fare
cap](https://www.bbc.com/news/live/cdx7z2wwe7qt) from three to two pounds
sterling appears to be his most feasible policy.

As Prime Minister Burnham settles into Downing Street, he will have to watch
out for his detractors.
